item.title: Belmont Park Got a $550 Million Makeover. Will Fans Show Up?
item.description:
The new Belmont Park, just outside New York City, reopens Friday not merely as a racetrack but also as a host for a range of events, including large concerts and intimate performances. At least that is the vision of the New York Racing Association, which bet $550 million on its makeover.

The organization could not have rebuilt it without a $455 million loan from the state that was championed by Gov. Kathy Hochul. She intends to be at a ribbon-cutting ceremony Friday morning about 14 hours after watching her hometown Buffalo Bills in their new $2.1 billion Highmark Stadium.

“From Buffalo to Belmont we are investing in sports, which is a point of pride for New Yorkers,” Governor Hochul said in an interview. “Live racing in a world-class, cutting-edge structure I thought was a smart use of land.”

Horse racing is surging as deep-pocketed owners are setting records for spending at horse sales, thanks to a tax break in President Trump’s major spending and tax bill that was signed into law last year. The provision — called a bonus depreciation — lets businesses immediately deduct the full cost of certain assets, like machinery and equipment, to enhance their cash flow.

It now applies to racehorses, and it is helping turn these animals into a hot investment for wealthy people. Last year, owners spent nearly $1.5 billion in North America in pursuit of fast racehorses, a nearly 21 percent increase from 2024.

New construction and renovation have also been done on signature racetracks in Kentucky and Maryland. But at a time when horse bets can be placed with a few taps on a phone, the big question is whether people will go out to spend a day at the races.

In its heyday, more than 20,000 people filled the Belmont Park building on weekends and the Belmont Stakes, the third leg of the Triple Crown, often drew more than 100,000. It was considered the grand old racetrack on Long Island with its mile-and-a-half oval and imposing grandstand.

The new Belmont Park was designed for a thriving sport with a more modest hold on the public. The five-story, 300,000-square-foot building accommodates 10,000 people in its seats, suites and restaurants, but can be expanded with temporary structures to handle the demand for the Belmont Stakes, which in recent years was held at the Saratoga Race Course and capped at 50,000 attendees. It offers a smaller, more European-style experience, with plenty of green space. And the building is ringed with balconies overlooking the paddock and the racetrack that also offer views of Manhattan.

While everyday horse players can still get general admission tickets for as little as $7, the prices get steeper for more premium experiences. Box-seat memberships go for $36,000 to $72,000 a year and include hospitality. Ninety percent of those seats have been sold, according to NYRA officials. More than half of the 32 Champion Suites, which can fit 16 to 50 people and start at $175,000 annually, have been sold on a multiyear basis. They also include food and drink and are equipped with flat screens and betting windows.

Marc Holliday, chairman of the NYRA board of directors, said the association’s goal was to “right size” Belmont Park with a modern design and to offer best-in-class hospitality and experiences. He said he wanted it to be different from Saratoga, which is one of the nation’s oldest sporting venues.

“Saratoga will always be known for its history and the nostalgic day of racing,” said Mr. Holliday, who is also chief executive of SL Green Realty Corp. “I wanted downstate to be something completely oriented toward the future and kind of a new beginning for horse racing.”

David O’Rourke, the chief executive of the NYRA, said the old Belmont Park, which opened in 1968, had been built strictly for gambling on horses. At the time, there were no competing casinos, and legalized sports betting was half a century away.

He said the downsized Belmont Park had been designed to be an “entertainment zone,” hosting big concerts in its infield or smaller performances, like plays, in the track’s paddock where horses are prepared before a race.

Mr. O’Rourke said the new Belmont would benefit from its neighbor, UBS Arena, home to the New York Islanders of the National Hockey League. The two now share a backyard, where the new Big Red’s sports bar offers easily accessible pregame hospitality for both venues.

“Now the intention will be to see how the patrons interact with it,” he said. “Is it the backyard where we’re going to have playgrounds and a kid’s zone? And as people start to experience it and use it, that’s how we’re going to move forward with the investment and the things that we’ll add to it.”

Still, for 10 months a year, Belmont Park’s main attraction will remain horse racing. The $455 million loan was given on the condition that the NYRA return Aqueduct racetrack in Queens and its more than 100 acres of land to the state. With the financing, the association razed the old Belmont and built four new racing surfaces: a renovated 1.5-mile oval along with two new grass tracks and a synthetic one that will host winter racing.

NYRA will repay the state $25.8 million annually for 20 years with money from its video lottery capital funds — a designated percentage of revenues from downstate facilities such as Resorts World New York City Casino at Aqueduct — to pay for race purses, capital improvements and operational support.

On Friday, the equine star of Belmont Park is Forever Young, a Japanese racehorse widely considered the best in the world. He has won more than $31 million in purses, racing in Japan, Saudi Arabia and the United States, and is the favorite to win the Jockey Club Gold Cup on Friday.

Forever Young’s handlers are impressed with the new facilities.

“Belmont Park is the best complex for training now in North America,” said Hiroshi Ando, racing manager for the horse’s owner, Susumu Fujita. “We have a lot of options with main track, training track, Tapeta track, small track.”

item.title: A New Prediction Market, Run by a Tribe and Powered by Kalshi
item.description:
It isn’t just states trying to restrain prediction markets over their legality. Several Native American tribes have also taken aim at what has become a rapidly growing betting business.

But one has gone the opposite way.

The Tunica-Biloxi Tribe of Louisiana plans to announce on Friday a prediction-market app powered by Kalshi, the $22 billion company at the top of the industry. The app would allow customers to bet on real-world events through a new business owned and operated by the tribe.

The partnership will thrust Tunica-Biloxi, a tribe of about 1,600 members based in central Louisiana, into the national debate over prediction markets, which allow users to bet on sports, the price of commodities and much more.

Nearly two dozen states have sued Kalshi and other prediction-market companies, arguing that they are skirting gambling laws and avoiding paying billions of dollars in tax revenue. Kalshi has argued that it runs what is essentially a derivatives platform, with its bets classified as “event contracts” and regulated by the federal authorities.

Other Native American tribes have taken the opposite approach of Tunica-Biloxi.

On Wednesday, a federal appeals court panel blocked Kalshi from offering contracts within the territories of two tribes in California that have not authorized prediction markets to do business on their lands.

Dani Lever, a spokeswoman for Kalshi, said in a statement, “We’re reviewing all of our options to address this decision, including appeal.”

This week, representatives from 17 Native American tribes met with the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, the federal agency that oversees prediction markets like Kalshi and Polymarket. Their concern: that the agency’s rule-making put the tribes’ sovereignty and core gaming operations at risk.

But Marshall Pierite, Tunica-Biloxi’s chairman, said in an interview that the new venture allowed his people to enter a rapidly growing financial market. It is a sector his tribe first entered more than 12 years ago with Mobiloans, a high-interest online lender.

He added that it could serve as a model for other tribes, especially those that do not have major casino operations. (Tunica-Biloxi also runs Paragon, a casino and resort in central Louisiana.)

“This is cutting-edge,” he said, adding, “It can create a plethora of opportunities that can change the lives of a lot of tribal citizens.”

Under the terms of their partnership, Kalshi will essentially provide the market infrastructure for the app. Kalshi will handle tasks including matching customers to event contracts, essentially wagers on topics like a sports game, the weather and more.

The two will split revenue from the arrangement, similar to partnerships Kalshi has struck with the likes of Coinbase.

“Prediction markets and tribal economic development don’t have to be a fight,” Tarek Mansour, a founder of Kalshi and its chief executive, said in a statement. He added, “Indian Country should have more paths to economic self-determination, not fewer.”

Helping make the venture possible was a decision by the C.F.T.C. on Thursday that cleared the way for apps to let users trade in derivatives the agency regulates.

Mr. Pierite said that he first began to study prediction markets as a potential business opportunity about eight to nine months ago and pursued a meeting with Kalshi through someone he described as a “mutual friend.”

Though Tunica-Biloxi nominated President Trump for the Nobel Peace Prize and Kalshi counts Donald Trump Jr. as an adviser and shareholder, Mr. Pierite said that no one in the Trump orbit had brokered the introduction. He declined to elaborate.

Mr. Pierite argued that while critics might now accuse Tunica-Biloxi of providing cover for Kalshi in its fights against states and other tribes, he believed in the prediction-market business model. He added that the two were firmly aligned, describing Kalshi as “Tunica-Biloxi ride or die.”

Would he publicly vouch for Kalshi? “Hell, yes,” Mr. Pierite said.

item.title: Meet Howard Buffett, the New Chairman of Berkshire Hathaway
item.description:
Howard G. Buffett is taking over as chairman of Berkshire Hathaway upon the retirement of his father, Warren E. Buffett, on Friday.

He will step into the shoes of the most famously successful investor of modern times.

The elder Mr. Buffett, 96, is known as the Oracle of Omaha for his prowess in picking winner after winner for decades.

The younger Mr. Buffett, 71, has been involved in several businesses and charitable causes and has served on Berkshire’s board since 1993.

Berkshire Hathaway is a trillion-dollar company that has made major investments in numerous large firms, including Geico, Apple and Coca-Cola.

Few expect drastic changes; Howard Buffett has been a director of Berkshire for 30 years. Gregory E. Abel, a longtime lieutenant, took over as chief executive last year.

Mr. Buffett, who goes by “Howie,” attended three colleges in the 1970s, Augustana College in Rock Island, Ill.; Chapman College in Orange, Calif.; and the University of California at Irvine. He did not graduate from any of them.

In 1986, he began running a 400-acre farm north of Omaha that his father purchased for him. As an incentive to encourage his son to be healthy, Warren Buffett took a percentage of the profit that was smaller if Howard, then 200 pounds, kept his weight below 182.5 pounds.

Howard now manages a 1,500-acre farm in central Illinois that is owned by his family, and still operates the 400-acre farm in Nebraska.

He became a vice president at the agricultural company Archer Daniels Midland, but resigned in 1995 because of concerns over how it handled price-fixing allegations.

He has been involved in other business and philanthropic activities, including starting a photography publishing company, Bioimages, and establishing a charitable foundation in his name. His foundation has provided hundreds of millions of dollars to Ukraine for efforts like mine clearing and improving infrastructure. He was a member of the World Wildlife Fund’s national council and a trustee of the Nature Conservation Trust, a charity he founded that works to protect the environment.

Mr. Buffett, the middle child of three, has been married to his second wife, Devon G. Morse, since 1982.

As Berkshire’s chairman, Mr. Buffett will lead the board of directors, who oversee the firm but don’t get closely involved in its day-to-day operations. Mr. Buffett will guard the company’s “culture and values — both worth more than anything on our balance sheet,” Warren Buffett said in a letter to shareholders on Friday.

“I feel I’m prepared for it because he prepared me,” Howard Buffett told The Wall Street Journal last year. “That’s a lot of years of influence and a lot of years of teaching.”

A Canadian who started as an accountant, Mr. Abel, 64, joined Berkshire in 2000.

He helped expand Berkshire Hathaway Energy and most recently ran other companies owned by the firm, including Brooks running shoes and a private jet service.

As chief executive for the past year, he runs the business and oversees Berkshire’s major investments. His key lieutenants are the main actors in selecting which companies to purchase.

The sprawling company is sitting on hundreds of billions in cash, meaning more acquisitions are possible.

Investors will be watching Mr. Abel closely as he begins the immense task of following in the footsteps of a towering figure like Warren Buffett.

Erik Gordon, a business professor at the University of Michigan, said last year, “Taking over from Buffett is harder than taking over from Superman.”

Warren Buffett’s investment fund purchased Berkshire, originally a textile company in Western Massachusetts, in 1964. Mr. Buffett turned it into a holding company, and expanded it far beyond its textile roots. It is based in Omaha.

It has owned See’s Candies, local newspapers, Dairy Queen, Benjamin Moore, Duracell and Fruit of the Loom, as well as companies in the furniture, jewelry, energy, railway, banking and housing sectors.

Its astonishing decades-long rise to a trillion-dollar company has been widely credited to Mr. Buffett’s sagacity in picking companies.

Mr. Buffett is regularly called the most successful investor of modern times, if not of all time.

Georgia Gee contributed research.

item.title: Uber to Pay $40 Million to Parents of Woman Fatally Hit by Car
item.description:
Uber Technologies Inc. has been ordered to pay $40 million to the parents of a woman who was fatally struck by a vehicle after a driver left her and a friend on a California freeway, an arbitration document and lawyer said.

On Aug. 12, 2023, the woman, Emily Normandin-Parker, 23, and her friend Luna Moore called an Uber to drive them home after a night out in Orange County, Calif., the document said. After Ms. Moore became sick and vomited, the driver, Vu Tran, pulled over on State Route 73 and stopped at a gore point, it said, referring to the triangular plot of land where a road forks at an intersection or ramp.

While stopped in an “unsafe and illegal” spot, Mr. Tran argued with Ms. Moore about a cleaning fee, the document said. He showed “no concern for Normandin-Parker’s whereabouts despite knowing she had exited the vehicle and was intoxicated,” it said.

Ms. Normandin-Moore wandered into traffic “in an inebriated state” and was struck and killed by a vehicle that was traveling 70 miles per hour, the arbitration document said.

The award was announced as the outcome of arbitration process conducted in March by Richard A. Stone, an arbitrator and retired judge, in Los Angeles. It touched on the legal extent to which Uber is responsible for the actions of its drivers, an issue that has arisen in other lawsuits.

The arbitration document was published on Thursday by the lawyers representing Ms. Normandin-Parker’s parents, Carol Normandin and Ken Parker.

The parents and Ms. Moore accused Mr. Tran and Uber of negligence, asserting that the company had liability as a common carrier. That classification applies to companies that provide transportation services to the public, obligating them to protect and warn passengers of any dangers.

Uber argued that, under California Proposition 22, Uber and Lyft drivers are classified as independent contractors and that the company merely “provides a software platform connecting riders with independent third-party drivers,” the document said.

But the arbitrator noted that Uber controlled key aspects of the rider experience, set fares and profited directly from rides. Uber, he found, was “vicariously liable” for Mr. Tran’s negligence because it had a duty for safety that cannot be delegated.

Ms. Moore also presented claims of intentional infliction of emotional distress against Mr. Tran.

Mr. Tran testified that he picked up the women from a bar early that Saturday morning and knew that they were inebriated, but not to what extent, according to the arbitration document. After Ms. Moore became sick and the women were told to leave the car, Mr. Tran testified that he called Uber within minutes and asked that Ms. Moore be charged a cleaning fee.

That demonstrated that Mr. Tran had a “single-minded fixation” on the state of his car and a lack of interest in the riders’ safety, the judge found.

Ms. Moore was awarded $300,000, the decision said.

Ms. Normandin-Parker’s parents “suffered immense loss” and were each awarded $20 million, the document said.

Lawyers for the family said in a statement that Uber had tried to keep the outcome of the arbitration and award confidential by proposing a settlement agreement that would have required the parents to pay a $10 million penalty for each time they discussed it publicly. The parents turned it down.

“You cannot claim to put safety first while fighting to silence the families whose lives have been devastated when that promise is broken,” the statement said.

Uber said it “ultimately did not pursue confidentiality” in the case.

The decision “makes clear that companies advertising safety cannot walk away from the responsibility that comes with those promises,” Rahul Ravipudi, one of the lawyers representing Ms. Normandin-Parker’s parents, said in the law firm’s statement.

In an emailed statement on Friday, Uber said that the driver no longer had access to the app, but that he had completed nearly 6,000 trips with a 4.96 rating, and “not a single incident involved unsafe drop-offs, freeway stops or rider injury.”

The company said that it was strengthening its approach to safety with new technology, policies and safeguards, including additional guidance to drivers about avoiding drop-offs in unsafe locations.

“While we respect the arbitration process, we believe the arbitrator was wrong in holding Uber legally responsible for the tragic events of that night,” it said.

item.title: Trump Says He Has Banned CNN, MS NOW and Politico From White House
item.description:
President Trump on Friday opened a new front in his ever-expanding battles with the news media, abruptly announcing a ban on CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House, even as it remained unclear how his prohibition would be enforced.

“There’s something wrong with a country that can allow people to write purposely negative stories,” Mr. Trump told reporters in the Oval Office, shortly after he announced his ban, “effective immediately,” in a post on Truth Social.

“Now, if they want to write them, that’s fine, but I don’t have to let them into my — into the people’s house,” the president added.

What Mr. Trump’s ban would mean in practice was not clear. The president’s remarks were vague — “I don’t want them in my office; I don’t want them here,” he said — and his aides did not immediately provide clarity. Journalists from those news outlets were working as usual on the White House grounds on Friday, and there were no signs of an imminent eviction.

Mr. Trump’s announcement was met with instant condemnation from many First Amendment groups, which called it unconstitutional. CNN and Politico both suggested they could mount challenges in court.

The White House Correspondents’ Association said in a statement that constitutional protections for the press do “not depend on whether the president likes a news organization’s coverage, agrees with its reporting, or approves of the questions its journalists ask.”

Presidents back to George Washington have complained about their press coverage, but Mr. Trump has increasingly attempted to control news outlets with a variety of bureaucratic levers and intimidation tactics. The president has filed lawsuits and used government tools like subpoenas to target newspapers, late-night talk show hosts, corporate media conglomerates and journalists whose reporting he dislikes.

In the Oval Office on Friday, Mr. Trump said he announced a ban “because they’re fake news.” He added, “You get sick of it.”

“If they could straighten themselves out, I’d love it,” he added.

Asked if his ban could survive a court challenge, Mr. Trump replied, “I don’t think that a court should allow fake news to be written day after day after day.”

Politico said in a statement that it would “vigorously defend our First Amendment rights,” and CNN called Mr. Trump’s ban “an illegal assault.”

“We have a right under the U.S. Constitution to do that reporting without hindrance or interference from the government,” said Emily Kuhn, a spokeswoman for CNN. A spokesman for MS NOW declined to comment.

In his post, Mr. Trump warned that he might add other organizations to his prospective ban, writing, “Other Fake News Media Outlets to follow.”

Mr. Trump expanded on those feelings at his Oval Office appearance, echoing the usual grievances that he unspools at rallies, news conferences and in interviews. “They purposely write negative news,” the president said. “And they do that because they want to try and diminish the Republicans and a Republican administration.”

Any prospective ban on journalists from specific news outlets would almost certainly prompt a legal challenge.

During Mr. Trump’s first term, he revoked a White House pass for Jim Acosta, the former CNN journalist. CNN succeeded in restoring Mr. Acosta’s press credentials in court.

This term, Mr. Trump has attempted to bar Associated Press journalists from parts of the White House, including the Oval Office and Air Force One. The A.P. has sued to restore its access, but that case remains in litigation; in the meantime, A.P. photographers have had continued access to the Oval Office. Its print journalists have had more limited access.

The Trump administration has also taken command of the daily White House press pool, a small, rotating group of reporters who relay the president’s daily activities to the public. Previously, the correspondents’ association chose which outlets participated.

In the Oval Office on Friday, Kelly O’Donnell, a White House correspondent at NBC News, said to Mr. Trump that every president takes an oath to uphold the Constitution, which includes the First Amendment, before asking how he justified this ban.

“I do, too,” Mr. Trump said of upholding the Constitution. “Much more so than you.” He then said he was banning the outlets “because they’re fake news.”

Jameel Jaffer, the executive director of the Knight First Amendment Institute at Columbia University, said that the ban floated by Mr. Trump on Friday is clearly unconstitutional because it would punish news organizations for the content of their reporting.

“If President Trump means to expel these news organizations from the White House press pool, his action is doubly unconstitutional because the press pool is a ‘public forum’ under the First Amendment, which means the president can’t exclude journalists from it on the basis of their viewpoints,” Mr. Jaffer said.

Tim Richardson, the journalism and disinformation director at PEN America, put it bluntly: “Someone needs to explain to President Trump how the First Amendment works.”

Zolan Kanno-Youngs contributed reporting from Washington.

]]>

item.title: Anthropic Moves Ahead With I.P.O. Plans Amid A.I. Safety Debate
item.description:
Dario Amodei, Anthropic’s chief executive, roiled Wall Street and Silicon Valley recently when he called for more guardrails on the pace of artificial intelligence development.

But even as Dr. Amodei became embroiled in a contentious A.I. safety debate, his company — which makes the Claude chatbot — continued to prepare for a blockbuster initial public offering that may shape up to be the biggest listing ever.

The company is expected to reach more than $100 billion in annualized revenue by the end of this year, according to four people familiar with the matter. That’s up from $65 billion in annualized revenue as of July. Investors seeking to get a piece of the I.P.O. are using those soaring numbers to justify Anthropic’s staggering potential valuation of $2 trillion.

The A.I. lab could publicly release financial documents detailing its offering as soon as in the coming weeks, which could put it on track for its shares to start trading as soon as November, said two people with knowledge of the situation who, like others quoted in this article, spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss the confidential plans.

The people stressed that the plans could still change. The timing of I.P.O.s are always subject to change because of factors like shifting investor sentiment and market volatility.

That is particularly the case for a company that is a leading force in an unpredictable industry in which many executives, including its own leader, are increasingly warning about sizable risks.

That the giant I.P.O. is plowing ahead highlights a broader tension surrounding A.I.: Despite worldly concerns about the technology’s disruptive powers, the returns these companies promise to investors are enormously tantalizing.

Going public could give Anthropic quick access to capital to help fund its large financial needs, in particular the substantial computing costs necessary to build and run its A.I. models.

Investors expect the company to have about five gigawatts’ worth of compute — the industry term for computing power — available to use by the end of the year, and would roughly double that capacity by the end of next year, according to three people familiar with the figures. That would put it on par with its rival OpenAI.

On Thursday, Anthropic hosted about 100 investors from venture capital firms at its San Francisco headquarters to discuss its technology offerings in a customer event, according to two people familiar with the event.

Jared Kaplan and Ben Mann, two of Anthropic’s co-founders, and Boris Cherny, the head of Claude Code, made presentations alongside Andrej Karpathy, a researcher and co-founder of OpenAI who joined Anthropic this year, the people said.

Anthropic’s bankers and its executives, including Dr. Amodei and its chief financial officer, Krishna Rao, have also met with potential investors in the I.P.O. in recent weeks. The company has taken meetings with those who are willing to write large checks, or are pre-existing investors in Anthropic, four people familiar with the discussions said.

Some smaller investors are hoping to invest at the I.P.O. but haven’t yet managed to obtain an audience with management, these people say.

In some of these meetings, the company has pointed to the positive aspects of artificial intelligence, including its research into biology and potential to cure diseases, according to three people familiar with the pitch.

When asked about the potential threat from China offering cheaper open-weight A.I. models — which publicly provide the underlying calculations of their systems — Anthropic has downplayed the competition. The company has told investors that only a small portion of businesses rely on such models, one person familiar said.

Several investors also said they believe Anthropic can expand its business even if it slows certain A.I. development, as Dr. Amodei recently called for. That’s because the company generates a majority of its revenue selling Claude to business customers, who are still early in their adoption of the technology.

Still, bankers and lawyers say Anthropic is wading through largely uncharted territory with its I.P.O.

Dr. Amodei’s safety warnings raise questions about potential liabilities for the company if, for example, a rogue agent leads to litigation. (These risks are not generally insured.) Dr. Amodei called for the development slowdown shortly after a former Anthropic researcher warned the chance that A.I. could make humans extinct within a decade was greater than 10 percent, creating more cosmic concerns.

“My experience is, it’s a bit like political risk, investors just kind of get their arms around it and just deal with it,” said Craig Coben, a former global head of equity capital markets at Bank of America.

Anthropic’s I.P.O. also raises questions about whether Dr. Amodei can ensure the safety of advanced A.I. models and withstand the pressures of running a publicly traded company that is subject to the whims of public investors clamoring for growth.

Some Anthropic investors argue that as a public company, it can achieve those goals simultaneously.

“Anthropic will IPO,” wrote Brad Gerstner of Altimeter Capital on social media on Sept. 12. He added, “And its beneficial / critical that we bring even more transparency, scrutiny, accountability, & participation to these grt American companies!”

As a public company, Anthropic would provide insights into its business, most notably its financials. It would also spread the wealth it generates beyond a handful of private shareholders, potentially giving more of the country a direct stake in the success and safety of A.I.

There may be limits to that transparency, said Jesse Fried, a law professor at Harvard Law School, who has studied Anthropic’s governance. Anthropic would still be able to keep some data — like what is transpiring in its lab — confidential.

“If you’re worried about, like, agents emerging from the testing dungeons of Anthropic and taking over the world, it doesn’t really help,” Mr. Fried said.

OpenAI is taking a different approach. Last week, its chief executive, Sam Altman, said the company was putting off its public listing until 2027. The company had already been weighing a 2027 listing as it shores up its finances and tries for a $1 trillion valuation. (It is in talks to privately raise funds at a $1.5 trillion valuation.)

(The New York Times has sued OpenAI and Microsoft, claiming copyright infringement of news content related to A.I. systems. The two companies have denied those claims.)

OpenAI’s delay may make it even more appealing for Anthropic to go public now, said Edward Best, a partner in capital markets at the law firm Willkie Farr & Gallagher, before any regulation forced broad change upon the industry.

“If you can get your valuation out, I would say strike while the iron’s hot,” Mr. Best said.

Maureen Farrell contributed reporting.

]]>

item.title: Trump Promotes Program to Reduce Medicaid Drug Prices
item.description:
President Trump announced on Friday that all 50 states said they wanted to participate in a program aimed at lowering the government’s costs for some prescription drugs covered under Medicaid, the health insurance program for lower-income Americans.

In remarks in the Oval Office, Mr. Trump framed the effort as a way for states to save money that he suggested could be reinvested in health care. During this midterm election season, he has trumpeted his efforts to reduce drug prices while appearing in swing districts in Pennsylvania, Michigan, New York and elsewhere around the country.

“This one thing alone should win us the midterms,” Mr. Trump said, reiterating a sentiment he has repeatedly expressed. He was flanked by top health officials and several Republican governors: Larry Rhoden of South Dakota, Tate Reeves of Mississippi and Sarah Huckabee Sanders of Arkansas.

The program, called Generous, is a regulatory experiment intended for Medicaid to achieve Mr. Trump’s longstanding goal of equalizing drug prices paid by the United States with those paid by other wealthy countries. Drugmakers that take part have agreed to align the prices they charge Medicaid for certain drugs with those in Britain, France, Germany, Italy, Canada, Japan, Denmark and Switzerland.

But it was not clear what effect the program would have. Drug companies already give Medicaid significantly lower prices than what American employers and other U.S. government programs receive. And Americans covered under Medicaid already pay only a few dollars, or nothing at all, to fill their prescription drugs. That won’t change under the new model.

Not all of the prescription drugs paid for by Medicaid will be included in the program. It will include only medicines that are part of deals that many of the largest drugmakers have reached with the Trump administration, according to a White House official. Those agreements have not been made public.

Public Citizen, a left-leaning advocacy group, said that Mr. Trump’s drug pricing actions represented a “charade” that was not helping Americans.

“Here’s the reality Americans are facing: high drug prices, rising health insurance premiums and restrictions on drug coverage,” said Peter Maybarduk, who focuses on access to medicines at Public Citizen.

In his second term, Mr. Trump has taken a number of steps aimed at reducing drug prices.

He has announced 26 deals with drugmakers to lower some of their prices and build factories in the United States in exchange for exemptions from his threatened tariffs. His administration has created a website, TrumpRx, meant to help people navigate to websites and pharmacies where they can use their own money to buy certain drugs.

Trump officials also negotiated deals to make obesity drugs available for $50 a month out of pocket for some people on Medicare, the government health insurance program that covers people 65 and over and some people with disabilities. Since the start of July, 600,000 people have signed up.

Critics say the moves represent minor, narrow concessions that have not dented drugmakers’ profits or meaningfully lowered the country’s enormous spending on prescription drugs.

For example, Incyte, a Delaware drugmaker, said in a regulatory filing last month that it would sell its blood cancer drug Jakafi to Medicaid through the Generous program at a price in line with prices in other wealthy countries.

The company reassured investors that it expected it would not be subject to other, more aggressive regulatory experiments that the Trump administration has proposed. It also said its participation would not meaningfully affect its profits this year or in the future.

item.title: Paramount Weighs Some Concessions in Bid to Finalize Warner Bros. Merger
item.description:
Paramount is in active talks to settle a lawsuit seeking to block its purchase of Warner Bros. Discovery, as it tries to avoid a costly fee triggered by delays in completing the deal, according to seven people with knowledge of the discussions.

A settlement would clear the way for a $111 billion acquisition that could transform Hollywood, resulting in a media and entertainment behemoth with control of two movie studios, the major news outlets CBS News and CNN and the streaming services HBO Max and Paramount+.

In talks with the 12 states that brought the lawsuit, led by California, the two sides have discussed measures to protect the editorial independence of CNN, said five of the people familiar with the discussions. They have also talked about the divestiture of some cable channels, including Comedy Central, according to two of the people.

The negotiations come as Paramount stares down a deadline that will make its purchase of the rival entertainment conglomerate more expensive. A provision written into the $111 billion deal requires Paramount to pay shareholders of Warner Bros. Discovery about $7 million per day beginning on Oct. 1 if the deal hasn’t closed by then.

A spokeswoman for Rob Bonta, California’s Democratic attorney general, said his office could not “confirm or deny whether settlement talks are occurring or their alleged substance.” A spokeswoman for Paramount declined to comment.

The Wall Street Journal earlier reported that Paramount and the state attorneys general were making progress toward a deal.

The ongoing battle over Warner Bros. Discovery has inflamed anxieties in Hollywood, which has already undergone generations of disruption in the span of a decade. The rise of streaming, the slow death of the cable bundle and the uncertainty around traditional moviegoing have put one of California’s iconic industries on edge.

The 12 state attorneys general argued in their July lawsuit that Paramount’s acquisition would concentrate too much power over cable channels and movie distribution under one corporate owner. Paramount has responded that Hollywood needs a counterweight to tech giants like Netflix that have come to dominate the film and TV industry.

Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín, of the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California, has scheduled the trial to begin in March.

Discussions over a possible settlement were touch-and-go in the months after the lawsuit was filed. A meeting between Mr. Bonta and Paramount scheduled for last month was scrapped after Mr. Bonta accused the film studio of leaking details of the negotiations to the press.

As the discussions stalled, Paramount has sought to ratchet up the pressure on Mr. Bonta. David Ellison, the studio’s chief executive, suggested that the company could leave California if the two sides didn’t reach a settlement, a move that could disrupt California’s already fragile film and TV industry. In recent years, already facing competition from other states offering generous tax incentives, California has lost a substantial amount of production to overseas destinations.

Against the backdrop of Mr. Ellison’s comments, prominent California Democrats, including Gov. Gavin Newsom and Mayor Karen Bass of Los Angeles, have expressed a preference for Mr. Bonta to settle the case.

In addition to the possible sale of Paramount’s cable channels and measures to protect the independence of CNN, negotiators have talked about enshrining in the settlement Paramount’s promise that the combined studios will produce 30 films a year, said two people familiar with the matter.

Over the past few months, tensions over the acquisition have been on display in public and in private.

On Monday, during the Emmy Awards at the Peacock Theater in downtown Los Angeles, Governor Newsom approached the actor Mark Ruffalo, an outspoken opponent of Paramount’s deal for Warner Bros., and delivered surprising news, according to two people familiar with the conversation.

Mr. Newsom told Mr. Ruffalo that he had just received a call from Mr. Ellison. Negotiations had stalled, Mr. Newsom said, and Paramount was possibly preparing to announce plans to leave California.

“This is a perfect example of a company doing everything wrong to get what they want,” Mr. Newsom said, according to the two people.

Izzy Gardon, a spokesman for Mr. Newsom, said that the comment was specifically about a dust-up over Mr. Ruffalo’s remarks on the Ellison family and Israel, not the company’s broader behavior during negotiations. The governor did not tell Mr. Ruffalo that Paramount was “definitely” leaving California, Mr. Gardon said, but was instead referring to “statements the company had made about possibly exiting California.”

Mr. Bonta, interviewed in New York on Thursday after speaking at The Atlantic Festival, suggested Paramount was trying to threaten the attorneys general into a settlement. He said leaving California would run counter to the company’s pledge to help revitalize the film and television business.

“If they choose to leave California after they professed their commitment to California and to the future of Hollywood, I would see that as being hypocritical,” Mr. Bonta said. He added that Paramount’s paying the $7 million daily fee if the deal was delayed was akin to “sleeping in” a bed that the company had made itself.
